settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Stiffness in the tendon first thing in the morning
  • Pain that warms up during activity and returns afterwards
  • Tenderness when you squeeze the tendon above the heel
  • Thickening or a tender lump along the tendon

The Achilles transmits everything the calf does into the foot. Pain there usually follows a change in load — more running, faster running, different surfaces or shoes — or a mechanical reason the tendon is working harder than it should.

image.alt: Diagram comparing a normal Achilles tendon with tendonitis, rupture and tendonosis

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram comparing a normal Achilles tendon with tendonitis, rupture and tendonosis</figcaption>
In detail
The Achilles tendon joins the calf to the back of the heel. Our assessment looks at which side of the tendon hurts, because each side points to a different way the foot is moving.

image.alt: A thickened Achilles tendon at the back of the heel

settings.editor: Which side of the tendon
Foot rolls in
Burning pain and inflammation on the inside of the ankle, behind the ankle bone. Rolling in puts extra strain on the inner tendon.
Rolls out, then in
Burning, sharp pain and swelling either side of the attachment, sometimes with a hard lump on the tendon.
Foot rolls out
Pain and swelling on the outer side. Often a high-arched foot that stays rolled out through the whole step.
01
The main difference is time. Tendonitis is short-term inflammation, often after a direct injury. Tendonosis is long-term, from repeated strain or an injury that has not healed.
02

settings.title: The name matters less than the cause

settings.editor: It matters less what the diagnosis is called than finding the biomechanical reason for it. That reason is what the treatment is aimed at.
03

settings.title: Why it should not be ignored

settings.editor: Over time, strain can cause small tears, scarring and adhesions in the tendon.
04
Orthotics (with forefoot additions where needed), shockwave, dry needling, manipulation and massage, and injection therapy.
How we diagnose it
Achilles Pain is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01

02
We work out whether the problem is the load, the mechanics, or both, and show you what we found.
03
Treatment addresses the mechanics alongside a graded loading plan, rather than rest alone.

settings.editor: What it is

A biomechanical assessment looks at how you stand, walk and load — not just the area that hurts. The Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment was developed here and draws on engineering principles to work out which structure is actually causing the pain.
Anyone whose pain has not settled, or who has been treated for the sore spot without the cause being found. It is the starting point for every other treatment on this site.
Where it is available

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s lower limb

settings.editor: In detail
The Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment (NBA™) was developed by Dr Abbie Najjarine to find the reason behind pain that has no injury behind it. It has three parts.

image.alt: Diagram of short leg syndrome and the body corrected to level

settings.editor: Assess, diagnose, treat
Assessment
Seven measurements of how your legs and feet are built and how they move.
Diagnosis
A biomechanical diagnosis: not just what hurts, but why it hurts.
Treatment
A plan aimed at that cause, then at easing the symptoms.
01

1. Heel position standing relaxed
  2. Heel position in neutral
  3. Shin twist, measured at the ankle
  4. Hip rotation, leg straight
  5. Hip rotation, leg bent
  6. Leg length difference
  7. Forefoot position (six types)
02

settings.title: Fixing the crack, or the foundation?

settings.editor: Think of a cracked wall. Patching the crack does not help if a tree root is lifting the foundation. The NBA looks for the foundation.
03

Which muscles have tightened or weakened to compensate, twists in the shin or thigh bone, a structural or functional leg length difference, and how the rear and front of the foot affect the rest of the body.
How it works here
Biomechanics is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We examine your alignment from the feet up, and watch how you move under load rather than only at rest.
02
We identify the structural or muscular irregularity causing the pain, and show you what we found before anything is prescribed.
03
Treatment is then prescribed against that diagnosis — orthotics, mobilisation, shockwave or a loading programme, depending on what the assessment showed.

settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• A gap between the knees when the feet are together
  • Feet that roll outwards, wearing the outer edge of the shoes
  • Tiring quickly, or complaints of aching legs after activity
  • In adults, aching on the outside of the knee or in the hip
  • Sometimes one leg more than the other

Some bowing is expected in young children and straightens as they grow. What matters is whether it is within the expected range for the age, and what sits above and below the knee. Where the angle of the hip joint sets the thigh bone more upright, the leg tends to bow and the foot to roll outwards, which makes the foot rigid and poor at absorbing shock. A leg length difference can also produce it on the shorter side only.
<figcaption>A school-aged boy running</figcaption>
How we diagnose it
Bow Legs is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess your child standing and walking, and measure the angle at the knees against what is expected for their age.
02
We look at the hip, the shin and the foot together, because the knee sits between them and usually reflects what they are doing.
03
Where nothing needs doing we say so and set a review. Where it does, treatment is staged around growth.

Questions

settings.title: Will my child grow out of it?

settings.editor: Often, yes — a degree of bowing is normal at certain ages and straightens on its own. The assessment is what tells you whether your child is within that range or outside it.

settings.title: Is it the same as knock knees?

settings.editor: They are opposites. Bow legs sit apart at the knees and are linked with a foot that rolls out; knock knees touch at the knees and are linked with a foot that rolls in. Both are assessed the same way.
Where the leg stays bowed, the load through the knee and the hip is uneven. In adults that is linked with wear on the outer side of the joint.
Where treatment is needed, it is usually orthotics to change how the foot loads, alongside hands-on work and stretches for the muscles that have tightened.
No. You can book directly.

settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• A bump on the inside of the foot at the base of the big toe
  • The big toe drifting across towards the second toe
  • Redness or rubbing where the joint presses on the shoe
  • Aching at the joint when walking or pushing off
  • Sometimes on one foot only

The first of the long bones behind the big toe is often naturally a little short, and sits angled in towards the middle of the body. For it to reach the ground, the foot rolls in. As it does, the ground pushes the big toe across and rotates it, and over time the muscles that pull the toe inwards shorten and hold it there. Where a bunion forms on one side only, a longer leg rolling in more than the other is often behind it.

image.alt: Diagram of the four stages of a bunion, from a normal foot to the tertiary stage

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of the four stages of a bunion, from a normal foot to the tertiary stage</figcaption>
How we diagnose it
Bunions is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess the foot as it loads, and measure the position of the first metatarsal and the big toe, rather than looking at the bump alone.
02
We identify what is driving the toe across — foot alignment, a short first metatarsal, a leg length difference, or footwear — and explain what we found.
03
Treatment is aimed at that cause, because a bunion that is not addressed mechanically tends to keep progressing through its stages.

Questions

settings.title: Will a night splint straighten it?

settings.editor: A night splint may ease the pain, but it will not correct the bunion. As soon as you walk again the mechanics that caused it are still there, and the drift continues.

Progression can usually be slowed where the cause is addressed early. By the later stages, once the joint has changed shape, the deviation itself is not reversible, which is why it is worth assessing before it gets there.
That is a decision for you and your surgeon. What we assess is the mechanical cause, which surgery does not change on its own.

settings.title: I have had bunion surgery. Do I still need orthotics?

settings.editor: Surgery corrects the toe; it does not correct the way the foot loads. Where that is left unaddressed, the bunion can return over the years that follow.

settings.title: Why have I only got one?

settings.editor: A one-sided bunion often points to a leg length difference, where the longer leg rolls in further. That is one of the things the assessment measures.

settings.editor: What it is
Children’s feet are still forming, and some things that look alarming settle on their own while others do not. An assessment tells you which you are looking at, and whether anything needs doing now.
Parents who have noticed in-toeing, out-toeing, flat feet, tripping, or a child who complains of sore legs after activity or at night.
Where it is available

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine examining a child’s feet

settings.editor: In detail
Children’s feet and legs are still forming. It is important to assess the child’s biomechanics rather than putting pain down to growing pains.

image.alt: Diagram of Sever’s disease at the heel growth plate

settings.editor: Common in growing children
Heel, age 8–14
Soreness at the back of the heel, worse after running and when getting up. Linked to feet that roll in or out, not only to growth.
Knee, age 13–17
A tender lump below the kneecap where the tendon pulls on the growing shin bone.
Any age
Often a twist in the shin bone, inherited from a parent.
01
Where in-toeing comes from a twisted shin, the body often hides it by tightening the hip muscles rather than correcting it. Measuring it is how you know.
02
Active, fast-growing children, more often boys, whose feet roll in or out and put repeated stress on the heel growth plate.
03
Orthotics, heel lifts, foot mobilisation, strapping and calf massage, reviewed as your child grows.
How it works here
Children's Podiatry is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess how your child stands, walks and runs, and compare that against what is normal for their age.
02
We explain what we found in plain terms, including when the answer is that no treatment is needed yet.
03
If something does need addressing, treatment is staged around growth and reviewed as they develop.

Questions

settings.title: At what age should my child be assessed?

settings.editor: There is no fixed age. If you have noticed something about the way they walk or they are complaining of pain, that is the time to have it looked at.

settings.title: Is in-toeing something they grow out of?

settings.editor: It often looks better with age. Where it comes from a twist in the shin bone, the body tends to hide it by tightening the hip muscles rather than correcting it, so measuring it is how you know. That is the reason to have it looked at rather than waiting.

settings.title: Do you have a clinic just for children?

settings.editor: Yes. Children are seen at all of our clinics.
Not necessarily. Many children need nothing beyond monitoring. Orthotics are only prescribed where the assessment shows they will change something.
No. You can book directly. If you are on a Medicare care plan your GP will refer you, and we can bill that.

settings.editor: What it is
A custom orthotic is made to your prescription, not picked off a shelf. It is designed to change the way load passes through the foot and up the leg, based on what the biomechanical assessment found.
People whose assessment shows the way they load the foot is driving their pain — commonly heel pain, arch pain, forefoot pain or knee pain that traces back to the foot.
Where it is available

image.alt: A custom orthotic device held against a patient’s foot

settings.editor: In detail
An orthotic is a device that changes the ground to suit the individual needs of the person, child or adult.

image.alt: Different styles of orthotic for different shoes

settings.editor: Three levels of orthotic
Minimal correction
A generic pre-made insole. It offers little correction, does not last long and does not correct the forefoot.
Customised pre-made
Moulded with heat to your ideal foot position, in soft, medium or firm densities.
Made from a cast
Made to a cast of your feet in the ideal position. Casts are taken standing, as they have been in our clinics since 1990.
01

settings.title: Matched to your foot and weight

settings.editor: How firm the orthotic needs to be depends on how far your foot rolls in and on your body weight. The higher of the two decides.
02
You might have one pair of glasses for driving and another for reading. Running shoes, work shoes and flats may each need a different style of orthotic.
03
The arch should not flatten like a pancake under thumb pressure, and the orthotic should sit stable on a flat surface. If it rocks, it needs balancing.
04

settings.title: Orthotics are not the whole plan

settings.editor: Tight muscles work like a kink in a hose, blocking the correction. Plans often add dry needling, massage, stretches, mobilisation or shockwave, sometimes for a few weeks before orthotics are made.
How it works here
Custom Orthotics is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment establishes what your foot is doing under load and why it is causing pain where it does.
02
The device is made to that prescription, not picked off a shelf.
03
You come back for fitting and adjustment. Orthotics are normally paired with footwear advice so the device is not working against your shoes.

Questions

settings.title: Will they fit in my normal shoes?

settings.editor: That is part of the prescription. Bring the shoes you wear most to your appointment so the device is made for them.

settings.title: How are these different from chemist insoles?

settings.editor: An off-the-shelf insole is a generic shape. A custom orthotic is made to a prescription from your own assessment, to change a specific problem the assessment identified.

settings.title: Do orthotics hurt to wear at first?

settings.editor: There is usually a break-in period. Your podiatrist will tell you how to introduce them and will adjust the device if needed.

settings.title: Can I claim orthotics on private health?

settings.editor: Yes, under most extras policies. We have HICAPS, so the rebate comes off at reception. Check your own limits with your fund.
